claims.text: Greater local atomic mixing in HEA nanoparticles increases cohesive stabilizing interactions.
Greater local atomic mixing delays premelting relative to local compositional segregation.
Greater local atomic mixing narrows the melting range relative to local compositional segregation.
The starting HEA nanoparticles are disordered, multielement solid solutions.
Two samples with identical overall elemental composition but different local mixing provide the intended controlled comparison.
Annealing followed by quenching can produce a highly homogeneous, maximally mixed HEA nanoparticle state.
An alternative thermal treatment can induce localized segregation and reduce atomic mixing.
Differences in local mixing can manifest as differences in chemical short-range order.
Atomic mixing raises local cohesive-energy barriers by distributing strain.
Configurational entropy associated with atomic mixing contributes to delaying premelting.
Local chemical segregation creates weak spots that cause earlier and more gradual melting.
Relative to the homogeneous baseline, highly mixed nanoparticles should have a higher premelting-onset temperature and a narrower melting interval.
Segregated nanoparticles should premelt at a lower temperature and exhibit a broader melting transition.
Rapid annealing and quenching freeze a homogeneous high-entropy state into the baseline nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship should hold near the melting point for HEA nanoparticles whose overall composition and particle size are controlled while local ordering varies.
In situ TEM or DSC can measure premelting onset and the melting-temperature interval under controlled heating.
The magnitude of the thermal shift may depend on the alloy system and the degree of segregation.
No detectable difference, or a higher and sharper melting transition in the segregated sample, would falsify the proposed directional relationship.
